title: A Promise Made at a Hospital Bedside
script: Wulan: [tired] Teguh, it's been eleven years since Father made you promise to look after the orchard, and lately I've noticed you looking at it like a debt rather than an inheritance.
Teguh: [honestly] Because most days, it functions as both simultaneously, and I'm not certain the two are as distinguishable as I once assumed they'd be.
Wulan: [gently] Nobody would think less of you for selling it, you know. Circumstances have changed considerably since that promise was made at his bedside.
Teguh: [firm] Circumstances changing is precisely the condition under which a promise is actually tested, though. An easy promise to keep was never really a promise at all.
Wulan: [curious] Even so, do you think Father, if he could see how much the orchard now costs you, would still hold you to the letter of it?
Teguh: [reflective] I've turned that exact question over more times than I can count, and honestly, I no longer think it's the right question to be asking.
Wulan: [surprised] What's the right question, then?
Teguh: [thoughtful] Whether I made the promise sincerely at the time, believing it, and whether my present discomfort is a reason or merely an excuse dressed convincingly as one.
Wulan: [considering] That's a harder standard than most people hold themselves to, Teguh.
Teguh: [wry] Probably. But a promise you only keep when convenient isn't a moral commitment; it's a preference wearing a promise's clothing for appearances' sake.
Wulan: [warmly] I suppose I've admired that about you longer than I've said so aloud, actually, though I worry it costs you more than anyone notices.
Teguh: [honestly] It does cost something, regularly. But I'd rather carry that particular cost than the different, quieter one of becoming someone whose word requires convenient weather.
Wulan: [thoughtful] And if the orchard fails completely, despite everything you've poured into keeping it alive?
Teguh: [steady] Then I will have failed at farming, not at the promise. Those are two entirely separate ledgers, and I intend to keep them that way.
Wulan: [gently] Father would have liked hearing you say that, I think, more than he would have liked the orchard surviving.
Teguh: [warmly] I hope so. It's mostly for him that I've stopped confusing the two.

quiz.question: What promise did Teguh make to their father eleven years ago?
options: To sell the family house
To look after the orchard
To care for his mother
To finish his education
quiz.explanation: Father made Teguh promise to look after the orchard, a promise made at his bedside eleven years earlier.

quiz.question: How does Teguh respond to Wulan suggesting the promise could be released given changed circumstances?
options: He agrees immediately and plans to sell
He argues that changing circumstances are precisely what test a promise's sincerity
He says the promise was never serious
He blames their father for the burden
quiz.explanation: Teguh argues that circumstances changing is precisely the condition under which a promise is actually tested.

quiz.question: What does Teguh decide is the 'right question' to ask about the promise?
options: Whether the orchard is profitable
Whether he made the promise sincerely and whether his discomfort is a reason or merely an excuse
Whether his father would forgive him for quitting
Whether Wulan approves of his decision
quiz.explanation: Teguh concludes the right question is whether he made the promise sincerely, and whether his discomfort is a reason or an excuse dressed as one.

quiz.question: How does Teguh distinguish a moral commitment from a mere preference?
options: There is no real difference
A promise only kept when convenient is a preference wearing a promise's clothing
Preferences are always stronger than promises
Only written promises count as commitments
quiz.explanation: Teguh says a promise only kept when convenient isn't a moral commitment, but a preference wearing a promise's clothing.

quiz.question: How does Teguh separate failing at farming from failing at the promise?
options: He sees them as identical failures
He treats them as two entirely separate ledgers he intends to keep separate
He believes failing at farming means failing the promise
He refuses to consider the possibility of failure
quiz.explanation: Teguh says if the orchard fails he will have failed at farming, not at the promise, calling them two separate ledgers.
